questions.question:
Given below are two statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Read and mark the correct options:

Assertion (A): The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita includes a specific provision for 'community service' as a punishment.

Reason (R): This reform aims to reduce jail time by introducing community service for petty offences.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Assertion (A): The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita includes a specific provision for 'community service' as a punishment:**

 
 
• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** is a proposed legislation that seeks to reform the criminal justice system in India. It aims to replace the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC).
 
• One of the significant provisions in this proposed law is the introduction of **'community service'** as an alternative punishment for minor and petty offences.
 
• This provision is intended to make punishments more constructive and rehabilitative rather than punitive, especially for minor infractions.
 
• Hence, the **assertion is correct**.
 
 
 
• **Reason (R): This reform aims to reduce jail time by introducing community service for petty offences:**
 
 
• The inclusion of **community service** in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is indeed aimed at reducing the burden on prisons and ensuring that minor offenders are not subjected to unnecessary jail time.
 
• This reform aligns with global practices where community service is used as a rehabilitative measure to prevent repeat offences and help offenders reintegrate into society.
 
• By focusing on rehabilitation, the provision also helps in decongesting prisons and ensuring that jail time is reserved for serious offences.
 
• Hence, the **reason is correct**, and it provides the correct explanation for the assertion.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Proposed Reforms in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita:**

 
 
• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is part of the reforms proposed by the Indian government to replace outdated laws like the Indian Penal Code (1860), the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973), and the Indian Evidence Act (1872).
 
• It introduces modern concepts of justice, including **victim compensation**, **fast-tracking trials**, and alternative punishments like community service.
 
• It focuses on reducing procedural delays and ensuring that justice is delivered swiftly and fairly.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Community Service:**
 
 
• Community service is widely used in countries like the **United States, United Kingdom, and Australia** as an alternative to imprisonment for minor offences.
 
• It allows offenders to contribute positively to society while also reflecting on their actions and learning accountability.
 
• This approach is particularly effective in cases involving youth offenders or first-time offenders, as it reduces the likelihood of their exposure to hardened criminals in prisons.
 
 
 
• **Important Features of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita:**
 
 
• Replacement of colonial-era laws with more relevant and contemporary provisions.
 
• Inclusion of victim-centric reforms, such as compensation mechanisms and protection of witnesses.
 
• Provisions to enhance the speed and efficiency of the justice delivery system.
 
• Focus on decriminalizing certain offences to reduce the burden on courts and prisons.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Implications of Community Service:**

 
 
• Community service as a punishment ensures that offenders contribute to societal welfare while serving their sentence.
 
• It reduces the stigma associated with imprisonment and helps offenders reintegrate into society after completing their sentence.
 
• This approach also helps in addressing the issue of overcrowded prisons and ensures that jail time is reserved for serious crimes.
 
 
 
• **Global Examples of Community Service:**
 
 
• In the **United States**, community service is often used as an alternative punishment for non-violent crimes, including minor drug offences and traffic violations.
 
• The **United Kingdom** incorporates community service in its sentencing guidelines for crimes like vandalism, theft, and minor assaults.
 
• In **Australia**, community service orders are issued as part of restorative justice programs, aiming to rehabilitate offenders while benefiting the community.

questions.question: The Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), India's planned space station, is proposed to orbit at what approximate altitude above the Earth's surface ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**400-450 km**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS):**

 
 
• The **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** (BAS) is a proposed space station by **India**, under the guidance of the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).**
 
• It aims to serve as a platform for **scientific research, space exploration, and technological experiments**.
 
 
 
• **Proposed Altitude:**
 
 
• The BAS is planned to orbit the Earth at an approximate altitude of **400-450 km**, which is within the **Low Earth Orbit (LEO).**
 
• This altitude is optimal for **human spaceflight missions** and scientific experiments due to **easy accessibility and reduced radiation exposure** compared to higher altitudes.
 
 
 
• **Low Earth Orbit (LEO):**
 
 
• LEO typically ranges from an altitude of **160 km to 1,000 km** above the Earth’s surface.
 
• It is widely used for **satellites, space stations, and human spaceflight missions** due to its proximity to the Earth's surface.
 
 
 
• **ISRO's Vision:**
 
 
• The development of BAS aligns with ISRO's vision of **strengthening India's space capabilities** and achieving **self-reliance in space exploration.**
 
• It is expected to be a significant step forward after the **Gaganyaan mission**, India’s first human spaceflight program.
 
 

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of Low Earth Orbit (LEO):**

 
 
• LEO is preferred for space stations like the **International Space Station (ISS)** due to its **moderate orbital speed** and **low energy requirements** for launching payloads.
 
• Satellites in LEO are used for **Earth observation, communication, and research**.
 
• The orbital period of LEO satellites is approximately **90 minutes to 2 hours**.
 
 
 
• **Space Stations Around the World:**
 
 
• The most notable space station currently in orbit is the **International Space Station (ISS)**, orbiting at an altitude of around **408 km**.
 
• China has developed its own space station, **Tiangong**, which also orbits within LEO.
 
• India’s BAS will add to the growing list of **national space stations**, showcasing its advancements in space technology.
 
 
 
• **Gaganyaan Mission:**
 
 
• India’s **Gaganyaan mission**, planned for launch in the near future, will be the country’s first crewed spaceflight mission.
 
• It is a precursor to the establishment of the **Bharatiya Antariksh Station**, as it will test technologies critical for human space exploration.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Altitude Comparison:**

 
 
• **200-250 km:** This is a lower range of LEO, but it is not ideal for long-term space station missions due to **higher atmospheric drag**.
 
• **400-450 km:** This range is suitable for stable orbits and long-term missions, as planned for BAS. *Correct answer.*
 
• **600-650 km:** Higher altitudes face increased **radiation exposure**, making it less suitable for human habitation.
 
• **850-900 km:** This range is used for specialized satellites, not for space stations, due to high energy requirements for reaching and maintaining the orbit.
 
 
 
• **Significance of BAS:**
 
 
• It will enable **advanced scientific research**, including microgravity experiments and space technology testing.
 
• BAS will place India among the few nations capable of operating their own **human spaceflight programs**.

questions.question:
A country's government reported the following figures in its annual budget:

Total Revenue Receipts = Rs. 50 lakh crore

Total Expenditure = Rs. 75 lakh crore

Borrowings = Rs. 20 lakh crore

What is the Fiscal Deficit of the government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rs. 25 lakh crore**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:** The fiscal deficit is defined as the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total revenue receipts, excluding borrowings. It represents the shortfall that needs to be financed through borrowing.
 
• The formula to calculate the fiscal deficit is: **Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - Total Revenue Receipts**. Borrowings are not included in revenue receipts.
 
• Based on the figures provided in the question:
 
 
• Total Expenditure = Rs. **75 lakh crore**.
 
• Total Revenue Receipts = Rs. **50 lakh crore**.
 
 
 
• Using the formula: Fiscal Deficit = 75 lakh crore - 50 lakh crore = **25 lakh crore**.
 
• The borrowings of Rs. 20 lakh crore are not included in the calculation of the fiscal deficit. Borrowings are used to finance this deficit and are not considered part of revenue receipts.
 
• Hence, the **fiscal deficit** of the government is **Rs. 25 lakh crore**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:**

 
 
• The fiscal deficit indicates the total borrowing requirements of the government.
 
• It is expressed as a percentage of a country's Gross Domestic Product (**GDP**) to give an idea of the economy's health.
 
• A higher fiscal deficit often indicates higher government spending, which can lead to economic growth but might also increase inflation and debt levels.
 
 
 
• **Components of Total Revenue Receipts:**
 
 
• **Tax Revenue:** Includes revenue from direct taxes like income tax and corporate tax, and indirect taxes like GST, customs duty, etc.
 
• **Non-Tax Revenue:** Includes revenue from dividends, interest, penalties, fees, etc.
 
 
 
• **Components of Total Expenditure:**
 
 
• **Revenue Expenditure:** Includes recurring expenses like salaries, subsidies, pensions, and interest payments.
 
• **Capital Expenditure:** Includes spending on infrastructure, machinery, and other long-term assets.
 
 
 
• **Borrowings:**
 
 
• Borrowings are used to finance the fiscal deficit and can include both internal borrowings (from domestic sources) and external borrowings (from foreign countries or international organizations).
 
• High borrowings can lead to an increase in debt servicing costs and impact the country's financial health.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Fiscal Deficit:**

 
 
• A large fiscal deficit may lead to inflation as increased government borrowing can lead to higher money supply in the economy.
 
• It can also impact the credit rating of the country, making future borrowings costlier.
 
 
 
• **Government Measures to Reduce Fiscal Deficit:**
 
 
• Increasing revenue through tax reforms and better compliance.
 
• Reducing unnecessary expenditures and ensuring efficient allocation of resources.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• In the Union Budget of India for **2023-24**, the fiscal deficit was targeted at **5.9%** of GDP.
 
• Efforts like the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** implementation aim to increase tax compliance and revenue.

questions.question: What happens to the resistance of a conductor as temperature increases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It increases**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Resistance of a Conductor:** Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric current. It depends on factors like material, temperature, length, and cross-sectional area.
 
• When the temperature of a conductor increases, the atoms within the material vibrate more vigorously due to the added thermal energy.
 
• This increased atomic vibration causes more frequent collisions between the electrons (which are responsible for the conduction of electricity) and the atoms in the conductor. *Hence, resistance increases with temperature.*
 
• The increase in resistance is more pronounced in metallic conductors, as metals typically have free electrons that interact strongly with the vibrating atoms when temperature rises.
 
• This relationship between temperature and resistance is mathematically expressed as: **R = R₀(1 + αΔT)**, where **R** is the resistance at temperature T, **R₀** is the resistance at reference temperature, **α** is the temperature coefficient of resistance, and **ΔT** is the change in temperature. *Hence, the resistance increases as temperature rises.*
 
• In contrast, materials like semiconductors and insulators may show a decrease in resistance with temperature, as their conduction mechanism differs. *Thus, this explanation specifically applies to conductors.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is It increases.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting Resistance:**

 
 
• **Material:** Different materials have different electrical resistivities. Metals generally have low resistivity, making them good conductors.
 
• **Temperature:** As explained, resistance increases with temperature for conductors due to increased atomic vibrations and electron scattering.
 
• **Length:** Longer conductors have higher resistance because the electrons face more obstacles during their journey.
 
• **Cross-sectional Area:** A larger cross-sectional area reduces resistance as it provides more space for electrons to flow.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Resistance is utilized in designing devices like **electric heaters**, where higher resistance generates heat.
 
• Conductors with low resistance, such as **copper and aluminum**, are widely used in electrical wiring.
 
• Temperature-dependent resistances are used in **thermistors**, which are sensors for temperature measurement.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Temperature Coefficient of Resistance:**

 
 
• The **temperature coefficient of resistance** (**α**) quantifies how much the resistance of a material changes with temperature. For metals, **α** is positive, indicating an increase in resistance.
 
• 
 
• 
• For semiconductors, **α** is negative, meaning resistance decreases with temperature.
 
 
 
• **Practical Examples:**
 
 
• **Electric Bulbs:** Filament resistance increases with temperature, causing the bulb to glow brightly.
 
• **Transmission Lines:** Resistance increases in transmission lines during hot weather, leading to energy losses.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a direct tax in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Corporate Income Tax**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Tax:** A direct tax is levied directly on an individual's or organization's income or wealth. It is paid directly to the government by the taxpayer. **Corporate Income Tax** falls under this category.
 
• **Corporate Income Tax:** This is a tax imposed on the income or profit earned by corporations or businesses. It is an example of a **direct tax** because the burden of the tax cannot be shifted to another entity.
 
• Examples of direct taxes in India include **Income Tax, Corporate Income Tax, and Wealth Tax**. These taxes are mandatory and directly affect the individual or entity paying them.
 
• **Indirect Taxes:** In contrast, taxes like **Goods and Services Tax (GST), Customs Duty, and Excise Duty** are classified as **indirect taxes**. These taxes are not paid directly to the government by the consumer but are instead collected by intermediaries (e.g., businesses) and passed on to the government.
 
• The **Corporate Income Tax** ensures that businesses contribute to the country's revenue system. It is calculated based on the profits of the company and varies according to the size and type of the corporation.
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST):** This is an **indirect tax** applied to the supply of goods and services. The burden of the tax is passed on to the end consumer, making it different from a direct tax.
 
• **Excise Duty and Customs Duty:** Both of these are also **indirect taxes**. Excise Duty is levied on the production of goods, while Customs Duty is imposed on goods imported into or exported from India.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Corporate Income Tax.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Corporate Income Tax in India:**

 
 
• **Corporate Income Tax** is levied under the **Income Tax Act, 1961**. The tax rate varies for domestic and foreign companies.
 
• For a **domestic company**, the tax rate is generally between **15% to 30%**, depending on factors like turnover and nature of business. Foreign companies are taxed at a higher rate, typically **40%**.
 
• Certain exemptions and deductions are provided to companies based on their contributions to specific sectors, such as infrastructure, Research & Development, and startups.
 
 
 
• **Indirect Taxes in India:**
 
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST):** Introduced in **2017**, GST replaced several indirect taxes like VAT, Service Tax, and Excise Duty. It is levied on the supply of goods and services and has rates ranging from **0% to 28%**.
 
• **Customs Duty:** This tax is levied on imported and exported goods to regulate trade and generate revenue for the government.
 
• **Excise Duty:** This was a major indirect tax on the production of goods within the country before GST. It is still applicable on certain products like petroleum and liquor.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Differences Between Direct and Indirect Taxes:**

 
 
• **Direct Taxes:** Paid directly by individuals or organizations to the government. Examples: Income Tax, Corporate Tax.
 
• **Indirect Taxes:** The burden of these taxes is shifted to the end consumer. Examples: GST, Customs Duty.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Corporate Income Tax:**
 
 
• It is a major source of revenue for the government and contributes to **economic development**.
 
• It ensures that corporations pay their fair share of taxes, promoting financial equity within the economy.

questions.question: Which institution played a key role in India's economic reforms by providing loans and policy guidance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**World Bank + IMF**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **World Bank** and **IMF (International Monetary Fund)** were instrumental in guiding and supporting **India’s economic reforms**, especially during the balance of payments crisis in **1991**.
 
• The **IMF** provided crucial **financial assistance** in the form of a loan to stabilize India's economy and help overcome the economic crisis.
 
• The **World Bank** supported India by providing **long-term developmental loans** and offering policy advice on key sectors such as infrastructure, poverty alleviation, and structural reforms.
 
• Both institutions emphasized **liberalization**, **privatization**, and **globalization** as part of the reforms to ensure economic stability and growth. This led to significant policy changes in India.
 
• The reforms included **deregulation of industries**, reducing the role of the public sector, and opening up the economy to foreign investments and trade.
 
• The economic assistance and policy guidance from the **World Bank** and **IMF** helped India transition into a **market-driven economy**, laying the foundation for sustained growth in the decades that followed.
 
• Hence, the **World Bank** and **IMF** played a pivotal role in shaping India's economic landscape during a critical phase of its development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **World Bank:**

 
 
• The **World Bank** focuses on providing long-term developmental loans to countries for projects like **infrastructure development**, **poverty reduction**, and **education**.
 
• It has been a key partner for India in its development journey, contributing to numerous projects in energy, health, and education.
 
• **Example:** The World Bank funded projects in India during the 1991 crisis to ensure structural adjustments and policy reform implementation.
 
 
 
• **International Monetary Fund (IMF):**
 
 
• The **IMF** provides **short-term financial assistance** to countries facing balance of payments crises.
 
• In 1991, the **IMF** extended a loan to India, contingent upon implementing economic reforms such as **trade liberalization** and reducing fiscal deficits.
 
• **Example:** The IMF helped India overcome its foreign exchange crisis by offering financial support and policy advice.
 
 
 
• **Key Aspects of Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• The reforms led by the World Bank and IMF focused on reducing the role of the government in economic activities and encouraging private sector participation.
 
• Important policy changes included **reducing trade barriers**, **removing licensing requirements**, and **promoting foreign direct investment (FDI)**.
 
• **Example:** The introduction of the **LPG (Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization)** model in 1991 reshaped India's economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Options Explained:**

 
 
• **SAARC + WTO:** **SAARC** (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) focuses on regional cooperation among South Asian countries, while **WTO** (World Trade Organization) deals with international trade rules. These organizations did not play a direct role in India’s economic reforms.
 
• **BRICS Bank + ADB:** The **BRICS Bank** (New Development Bank) was established in 2014, much after India’s 1991 reforms. The **ADB** (Asian Development Bank) provides financial and technical assistance to Asia-Pacific countries but was not the primary driver of India’s reforms.
 
• **UNDP + UNESCO:** **UNDP** (United Nations Development Programme) and **UNESCO** (United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization) focus on developmental and cultural activities, not economic restructuring or policy reforms.

questions.question: What is the aim of launching the 'One Nation, One Ration Card ' scheme ?

options.text: Unifying the voter list across states
Providing universal access to subsidized foodgrains
Creating a uniform syllabus for schools
Providing a single tax system across India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Providing universal access to subsidized foodgrains**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **One Nation, One Ration Card (ONORC) Scheme:** The ONORC scheme was launched by the Government of India to ensure that all beneficiaries under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) can access subsidized foodgrains from anywhere in the country. It is a step toward promoting national portability of ration cards.
 
• The scheme enables migrant workers and their families to claim their entitled food grains at subsidized rates from any fair price shop (FPS) across India, irrespective of their home state. *Hence, the aim is to provide universal access to subsidized foodgrains.*
 
• The portability feature under ONORC is supported through the integration of the Public Distribution System (PDS) with technology like Aadhaar authentication and the use of an electronic Point of Sale (ePOS) system.
 
• This scheme eliminates the need for beneficiaries to reapply for a ration card when they move to a different state or union territory, ensuring food security even for the most vulnerable sections of society.
 
• The scheme is especially beneficial for **migrant workers**, who often face challenges in accessing food subsidies due to the lack of a locally issued ration card. *Hence, the statement aligns with the aim of the scheme.*
 
• This initiative is aligned with the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2, which aims to end hunger and ensure food security for all by 2030.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Providing universal access to subsidized foodgrains.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of the ONORC Scheme:**

 
 
• The scheme was first implemented in **August 2019** and was gradually expanded to cover all states and union territories by **July 2021**.
 
• It leverages technology to ensure the portability of ration cards. Beneficiaries can authenticate their identity using their **Aadhaar number** and avail of their food grain entitlement.
 
• Under the scheme, both inter-state and intra-state portability of ration cards are allowed, providing flexibility and convenience to beneficiaries.
 
 
 
• **Implementation and Technology:**
 
 
• The scheme uses an **Integrated Management of Public Distribution System (IM-PDS)** to track and monitor transactions across states.
 
• The ePOS devices installed at FPS ensure real-time authentication and prevent leakages or corruption in the system.
 
• **Aadhaar linkage** is a critical component of the ONORC scheme, ensuring that only eligible beneficiaries access the subsidies.
 
 
 
• **Benefits:**
 
 
• Provides food security to millions of migrant workers and their families.
 
• Promotes transparency, reduces corruption, and ensures the efficient delivery of benefits to the intended beneficiaries.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Options Explained:**

 
 
• Option 1: **Unifying the voter list across states** – This is incorrect as the ONORC scheme is unrelated to the electoral process or voter lists.
 
• Option 3: **Creating a uniform syllabus for schools** – This option pertains to education reforms and is not the aim of the ONORC scheme.
 
• Option 4: **Providing a single tax system across India** – This is related to taxation policies like the Goods and Services Tax (GST), not ration card portability.
 
 
 
• **Significance of ONORC:**
 
 
• It ensures the right to food, a fundamental right under Article 21 of the **Indian Constitution**, is safeguarded for every citizen, including the marginalized.
 
• The scheme strengthens the existing Public Distribution System and aligns with the government's broader agenda of inclusive growth and poverty alleviation.

questions.question: Which law prevails in case of a conflict between Union and State laws on a subject in the Concurrent List?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Union law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the case of a conflict between **Union and State laws** on a subject in the **Concurrent List**, the **Union law prevails** as per **Article 254(1) of the Indian Constitution**.
 
• The **Concurrent List** includes subjects where both the Union and State governments can legislate. However, in case of inconsistency, the **Union law** will supersede the State law.
 
• If a State law receives the **President's assent** under **Article 254(2)**, it can prevail over Union law in that particular state. However, Parliament retains the power to override such state laws by making a law on the same subject. *Hence, Union law takes precedence in most cases.*
 
• The primary purpose of giving precedence to Union law is to maintain **uniformity** across the country on matters of national importance.
 
• This principle ensures that there is no conflict in laws affecting citizens across different states and facilitates a cohesive legal framework. *Hence, the correct answer is Union law.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 254 of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• **Article 254(1)**: When there is a conflict between a law made by the Parliament and a law made by the State Legislature on a subject in the **Concurrent List**, the law made by Parliament shall prevail.
 
• **Article 254(2)**: If a State law on a Concurrent List subject conflicts with an existing Union law, and the State law receives the **President's assent**, the State law can prevail in that particular state. However, the Parliament can override the State law by making another law on the same subject.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• The **Concurrent List** is one of the three lists in the **Seventh Schedule** of the Constitution. It includes subjects where both the Union and State legislatures can legislate.
 
• Examples of subjects in the Concurrent List include **education, criminal law, marriage and divorce, bankruptcy, forests, and protection of wildlife**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Union Law Supremacy:**
 
 
• The supremacy of Union law ensures that there is a **uniform legal system** on subjects of national importance, avoiding discrepancies between states.
 
• This principle also ensures that the Union government can address issues of national interest effectively without being constrained by conflicting State laws.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Considerations in Article 254:**

 
 
• The **Concurrent List** subjects require careful legislation to avoid conflicts. Parliament has the final authority to ensure uniformity in laws.
 
• The **President's assent** is critical when State laws conflict with Union laws. This provides a constitutional mechanism to resolve conflicts.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Union Law Supremacy:**
 
 
• The Union government enacted the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**, which superseded State laws on environmental protection for uniform implementation across India.
 
• In the case of **education policies**, the Union government has consistently framed laws to ensure a standard education system across states, even when State laws differed.

questions.question: If someone becomes a minister or the Prime Minister without being a Member of Parliament, they must get elected to the Parliament within _______ months or they will have to vacate the office.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**six months**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 75(5)** of the **Indian Constitution** states that a person who is not a Member of Parliament (MP) can still be appointed as a minister, including the **Prime Minister**. However, such a person must become an MP within a period of **six months** from the date of their appointment.
 
• If the appointed person fails to get elected to either the **Lok Sabha** or the **Rajya Sabha** within this six-month period, they must resign from their ministerial position. Hence, option 2 is correct.
 
• This provision ensures that the **executive branch** remains accountable to the legislative branch, which is a crucial aspect of the **parliamentary system of governance**.
 
• The rule applies to both the **Union government** (Prime Minister and Union Ministers) and the **state governments** (Chief Ministers and State Ministers).
 
• The six-month provision allows flexibility in governance, ensuring that capable individuals can assume key positions temporarily even if they are not immediately elected members of the legislature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 75 of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• **Article 75(1):** It states that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, and the other ministers are appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister.
 
• **Article 75(5):** It mandates that a minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament must become a member within six months of their appointment.
 
• This article ensures that the **executive branch** is accountable to the **legislature**, which is a cornerstone of India's parliamentary democracy.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Application:**
 
 
• **PV Narasimha Rao:** He was appointed as the **Prime Minister** in 1991 and contested elections to become a member of the Parliament within six months.
 
• **Jayalalithaa:** In 2001, she was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu but had to resign after being disqualified from contesting elections.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary System of Government:**
 
 
• India follows a **parliamentary system of governance**, where the executive is responsible to the legislature.
 
• The system ensures that ministers, including the Prime Minister, remain answerable to the Parliament, reinforcing the principles of **democracy** and **accountability**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Legal Considerations:**

 
 
• The six-month provision is crucial in allowing the government to function smoothly while ensuring that all executive members hold a legitimate mandate from the legislature.
 
• The **President of India** plays a key role in appointing ministers, including individuals who are not MPs, based on the advice of the Prime Minister.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Six-Month Rule:**
 
 
• It provides a mechanism for appointing non-legislators as ministers or Prime Minister temporarily, ensuring that governance is not hindered.
 
• This provision has been used multiple times in India, highlighting its practical importance in the country's political framework.

questions.question: According to the 2024 GHI, what is India's child wasting rate, and how does it compare globally ?

__
 
• **India's child wasting rate** as per the **2024 Global Hunger Index (GHI)** is **18.7%**. This refers to the proportion of children under the age of five who have a low weight-for-height, indicating acute undernutrition.
 
• Child wasting is one of the four key indicators used in calculating the **Global Hunger Index**, alongside child stunting, child mortality, and undernourishment.
 
• The rate of **18.7%** places India among the worst-performing countries globally in terms of child wasting, highlighting a significant challenge in addressing acute child malnutrition. Hence, option 3 is correct.
 
• **Child wasting** is a critical health indicator as it represents a child's immediate nutritional status and their vulnerability to illness and mortality.
 
• Globally, the average child wasting rate is much lower than India's, emphasizing the country's lagging position in this area. *Hence, the correct answer is 18.7%.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Global Hunger Index (GHI):**

 
 
• The **Global Hunger Index** is an annual report that tracks hunger and malnutrition across countries. It is jointly published by **Concern Worldwide** and **Welthungerhilfe**.
 
• The index uses four indicators: **undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting, and child mortality** to measure and rank hunger levels globally.
 
• A higher GHI score reflects worse hunger conditions in a country.

• Wasting is defined as low weight-for-height. It usually indicates **acute malnutrition**, often caused by insufficient food intake or illnesses like diarrhea.
 
• Wasted children are at a higher risk of mortality and long-term developmental issues.

• **India's Position:**
 
 
• India has consistently reported high levels of child wasting in recent GHI reports, reflecting persistent challenges in public health and nutrition.
 
• Contributing factors include **poverty, food insecurity, lack of healthcare access, and poor sanitation.**

• **Other GHI Indicators:**

 
 
• **Child Stunting:** Refers to low height-for-age and indicates chronic malnutrition.
 
• **Child Mortality:** Measures the mortality rate of children under five, often linked to malnutrition and poor health services.
 
• **Undernourishment:** Refers to the proportion of the population with insufficient caloric intake.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• India has implemented programs like **POSHAN Abhiyaan** to combat malnutrition and improve child health indicators.
 
• Efforts such as the **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** and **Mid-Day Meal Scheme** aim to address child hunger and malnutrition.

questions.question: What characterizes Stage II of demographic transition?

options.text: Birth and death rates are equa
Death rate declines, birth rate remains high
Birth rate falls below death rate

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Death rate declines, birth rate remains high**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Stage II of the Demographic Transition:** This stage is characterized by a significant **decline in the death rate** while the **birth rate remains high**. This leads to a rapid increase in the population.
 
• The decline in the death rate is primarily due to **improvements in healthcare, sanitation, and nutrition**. For example, advancements in medical technology and widespread vaccination programs reduce mortality rates significantly.
 
• The birth rate remains consistently high during this stage due to **cultural and societal norms**, lack of awareness about family planning, and the reliance on large families for economic support. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• **Population Growth:** The result of this disparity between high birth rates and declining death rates is a **sharp increase in population**. This is often referred to as a "population explosion."
 
• In this stage, countries experience a **demographic momentum**, where population growth accelerates before stabilizing in subsequent stages.
 
• **Historical Examples:** Countries like **India and many African nations** went through Stage II during the mid-20th century when modern medical practices and public health measures were introduced.
 
• *Thus, the characteristic feature of Stage II is the significant decline in the death rate while the birth rate remains high, leading to rapid population growth.*

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information____ __**

__
 
• **Demographic Transition Model:**

 
 
• **Demographic transition** is a model that describes the transition of a country’s population from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as it develops economically and socially.
 
• The model has **four stages**:
 
 
• **Stage I:** High birth and death rates, leading to a stable and low population.
 
• **Stage II:** Decline in death rates, while birth rates remain high, causing rapid population growth.
 
• **Stage III:** Decline in birth rates, leading to a slowdown in population growth.
 
• **Stage IV:** Low birth and death rates, resulting in a stable or declining population.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Key Factors Influencing Stage II:**
 
 
• The decline in death rates is driven by factors such as **improved medical care, better sanitation, and increased food production.**
 
• High birth rates persist due to **cultural, social, and economic factors**, including the need for labor in agricultural economies and lack of family planning awareness.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Countries in Stage II:**
 
 
• **Historical Examples:** During the 19th century, countries like **England** and **Germany** entered Stage II due to the Industrial Revolution.
 
• **Contemporary Examples:** Many **developing countries**, including parts of Africa and South Asia, are currently in Stage II.
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points____ __**

 
• **Stage I vs. Stage II:**

 
 
• **Stage I:** High birth and death rates result in a stable population. Examples include pre-industrial societies.

questions.question: Which metal casting technique was mastered by ancient Indian sculptors?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cire-perdue (lost-wax casting)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cire-perdue**, also known as the **lost-wax casting technique**, was widely practiced by ancient Indian sculptors. This method involves creating a duplicate metal sculpture from an original wax model.
 
• The process begins by sculpting the desired object in wax, which is then coated with clay or other refractory materials to create a mold. The mold is then heated to melt the wax, which is "lost" or drained away, leaving a cavity in its place.
 
• Molten metal (usually bronze or copper alloys) is poured into the cavity, allowed to cool, and then the outer mold is broken away to reveal the final sculpture. This method is highly precise and allows for intricate detailing. *Hence, this is the correct technique mastered by ancient Indian sculptors.*
 
• Ancient Indian artisans, particularly during the **Chola dynasty** (9th–13th centuries CE), were renowned for producing exquisite bronze statues using this technique. Examples include the famous **Nataraja (Lord of Dance) sculptures**.
 
• This technique was not limited to religious or spiritual sculptures but was also used for crafting utilitarian objects and decorations. *Hence, the mastery of Cire-perdue by Indian sculptors is historically significant.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hammer forging:**

 
 
• Hammer forging is a technique where metal is shaped by hammering it into the desired form, usually while it is hot. This method is not suitable for intricate sculptures but is primarily used for tools, weapons, and other functional items.
 
• It does not offer the precision and detailing achievable with the lost-wax casting technique. Hence, this was not the primary technique mastered by ancient Indian sculptors.
 
 
 
• **Die-casting:**
 
 
• Die-casting is a modern industrial process where molten metal is forced into a mold cavity under high pressure. It is used for mass production of parts and components in industries such as automotive and electronics.
 
• This technique was not used in ancient India, as it requires advanced technology and equipment that were unavailable during that time.
 
 
 
• **Sand casting:**
 
 
• Sand casting involves creating a mold from sand and pouring molten metal into it. While it is a traditional technique, it does not allow for the fine detailing that Cire-perdue provides.
 
• This method is more suited for larger, less intricate objects, such as industrial components or simple sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Cire-perdue:**
 
 
• This technique has been used to create statues, jewelry, and other intricate artifacts worldwide, including in regions like Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece, in addition to India.
 
• In modern times, lost-wax casting is still used in art and jewelry making, demonstrating its enduring significance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• The Cire-perdue technique has been a hallmark of ancient Indian craftsmanship, particularly in regions such as Tamil Nadu and Odisha.
 
• The Chola bronze sculptures are UNESCO-recognized cultural artifacts and are considered masterpieces of world art.
 
 
 
• **Modern Adaptations:**
 
 
• Today, the technique is used with advanced materials and tools, but the core principles remain unchanged from ancient practices.
 
• Lost-wax casting continues to inspire artists and is integral to the production of fine art and jewelry globally.
